title_en: Fragments on the Letter to the Romans
author: Eusebius of Emesa
occasion: Eusebius explains difficult passages in Romans 7, arguing that Paul speaks there in an assumed persona to refute those who love sin and blame the flesh for evil.
argument: Eusebius argues that Paul's confessions in Romans 7 are spoken in an assumed persona, not in his own voice, for the refutation of those who love sin. He maintains that 'sin' in this passage means the devil, not a substance or the human flesh, and that the law and commandment remain holy, just, and good. The flesh itself is not evil by nature; rather, the devil dwelling in sinners is the agent of evil. Christians buried with Christ in baptism have been freed from this 'sin' and from condemnation.

outline.move: Paul speaks in an assumed persona in Romans 7 to refute lovers of sin, and 'flesh,' 'law,' 'sin,' and 'death' can name the devil rather than created realities.
The persona's words fit neither Paul nor the baptized, who are freed from Adam's condemnation; 'sin' is not a substance but a name for the devil, who used the commandment to deceive Adam.

The law and commandment remain holy, just, and good even though the devil became exceedingly sinful through them; Eusebius now interprets the 'I' of Romans 7 into the person of Adam, and death's reign began from disobedience.
The flesh is not evil by nature, since willing and choosing belong to the soul; the indwelling sin is the devil, who prepares evil in the heart as the Holy Spirit cooperates with the virtuous.

cast.name: Paul
cast.who: The apostle whose words in Romans 7 Eusebius interprets as spoken in an assumed persona.

cast.name: Adam
cast.who: The first human, whose disobedience brought death and whose voice Eusebius hears in Romans 7.

cast.name: the devil
cast.who: The originator and father of sins, called 'sin' by Paul and said to dwell in sinners.

cast.name: Christ
cast.who: The Son of God, whose obedience and death free believers from sin and death.

voices.speaker: Paul (assumed persona)
voices.how_marked: Eusebius says Paul speaks 'in an inserted persona' (ἐν παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ) and by impersonation (προσωποποιΐα), quoting Romans 7.

voices.speaker: Adam (as the 'I' of Romans 7)
voices.how_marked: Eusebius states that the passage is now interpreted 'into the person of Adam' (εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον).

key_terms.sense: In Romans 7, not a substance or mere act, but a name for the devil as originator of sins.
Sometimes the physical flesh, but in Paul's usage often a name for the devil or the old life of disobedience.
The Mosaic law and commandment, holy and good, though the devil used it as an occasion for sin.
Both common physical death and the spiritual death that entered through Adam's disobedience.
The rhetorical device by which Paul speaks in the character of another person.
Adam's disobedience, through which sin and death entered and reigned.
The condemnation from which those in Christ Jesus are freed.
The specific commandment given to Adam, holy, just, and good, though used by the devil to deceive.
The personal enemy of God and humans, also called Satan, Beliar, serpent, lion, sin, and death.
To work out or prepare beforehand, used of the devil preparing sin in the heart.

scripture: The author cites Romans and Genesis from the Septuagint tradition. Psalm numbering follows the Septuagint where applicable. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and verse numbering, with Septuagint Psalms noted as LXX where they differ from the Hebrew.
uncertain: The precise date of composition within Eusebius of Emesa's lifetime.
Whether the fragments formed a continuous commentary or separate homiletic notes.
The original extent and structure of the work from which these fragments survive.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἰθ' οὕτως ἤρξατο πάλιν τῆς καθ' ὑπόθεσιν προσωποποιΐας, ἀρξάμενος ἀπὸ τοῦ τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ὁ νόμος ἁμαρτία; μὴ γένοιτο· ἕως τοῦ ταλαίπωρος ἐγὼ ἄνθρωπος, τίς με ῥύσεται ἐκ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ θανάτου τούτου;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The assumed persona extends through u01-rem-mid as well; Eusebius explicitly says Paul 'began again' (ἤρξατο πάλιν) the prosopopoeia from 'What then shall we say?' through 'wretched man that I am,' and in u01-rem-mid he interprets 'I' as Adam's person (εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον ἐξηγεῖται), showing the persona continues.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Οἶδα δὲ ὅτι οὐκ οἰκεῖ ἐν ἐμοί, τοῦτ' ἔστιν ἐν τῇ σαρκί μου, ἀγαθόν. νῦν εἰς τὸ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ πρόσωπον ἐξηγεῖται.
_unresolved_facts.fix: Adam is identified as the 'I' specifically for the passage 'I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh' (Rom 7:18), but the broader prosopopoeia continues; the brief should note that Adam is one specific identification within the larger assumed persona, not a separate voice replacing Paul's persona entirely.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οὕτω δὴ καὶ τὸν διάβολον οὐ μόνον σατανᾶν καὶ ἀντικείμενον καὶ διάβολον καὶ ὄφιν καὶ λέοντα καλεῖν οἶδεν καὶ Βελίαρ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The source forms should include 'ἀντικείμενον' (the opposing one/adversary), which appears in the list between σατανᾶν and διάβολον.

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-early move: 'The persona's words fit neither Paul nor the baptized, who are freed from Adam's condemnation; 'sin' is not a substance but a name for the devil, who used the commandment to deceive Adam.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐπειδὴ δὲ ὁ θεῖος ἀπόστολος οὐχ ἁπλῶς ἁματημάτων, ἀλλ' ἁμαρτίας γενικωτάτης ἐχούσης φρόνημα, ἐχούσης νόμον, δυναμένης σοφίσασθαι, ἀφορμὰς πορίσασθαι πρὸς τὴν τοῦ κακοῦ κατασκευὴν μνημονεύει, οὐκ ἄλλον τινὰ γενικωτάτως ἁμαρτίαν ὀνομάζει, ἀλλ' ἢ αὐτὸν τὸν τῶν ἁματημάτων ἀρχηγέτην καὶ πατέρα διάβολον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The outline should specify that 'sin' as a generic term with 'mind' (φρόνημα), 'law,' and ability to deceive is identified with the devil—not that 'sin' in every usage means the devil. Eusebius distinguishes generic 'sin' from particular sins (ἁμαρτημάτων).

_unresolved_facts.claim: u01-rem-close move: '...as the Holy Spirit cooperates with the virtuous.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὥσπερ τοίνυν ταῖς φιλαρέτοις ψυχαῖς τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα συγκοπιᾶν λέγεται κατὰ τὸ περισσότερον πάντων ἐκοπίασα, οὐκ ἐγὼ δὲ ἀλλ' ἡ χάρις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ σὺν ἐμοί
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Holy Spirit 'co-toils' (συγκοπιᾶν) with virtuous souls, not merely 'cooperates'; and Eusebius cites Paul's 'I labored more than all, yet not I but the grace of God with me' to show this co-laboring, which the brief should reflect more precisely.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Eusebius argues that Paul's confessions in Romans 7 are spoken in an assumed persona, not in his own voice, for the refutation of those who love sin.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀλλὰ ταῦτα καὶ ὅσα τοιαῦτα ἐν παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ ὑποκρινόμενος λέγει πρὸς ἔλεγχον τῶν φιλαμαρτημόνων
_unresolved_facts.fix: The argument should specify that Paul speaks 'in an inserted persona' (ἐν παρενθέτῳ προσώπῳ) by way of 'impersonation/acting' (ὑποκρινόμενος)—the brief's 'assumed persona' is acceptable but misses the theatrical/performative nuance of ὑποκρινόμενος (acting a part).

_unresolved_facts.claim: The flesh itself is not evil by nature; rather, the devil dwelling in sinners is the agent of evil.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἀπελογήσατο διὰ τούτου τοῦ λογίου, ὅτι περ οὐ φαύλη κατὰ φύσιν ἡ σάρξ· οὐ γὰρ ἡ σὰρξ ἣν περικείμεθα οἰκεῖ ἐν ἡμῖν, ἀλλ' ὁ ἐν τοῖς παρανόμοις οἰκῶν διάβολος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The argument should include Eusebius's specific defense that 'the flesh which we wear' (ἡ σὰρξ ἣν περικείμεθα) does not dwell in us, but the devil dwelling in lawbreakers does—distinguishing between physical flesh and the 'sin' that dwells.
